description: Beyond Earth, Beyond Limits — We Engineer the Impossible.”
summary:
We developed an interactive educational website called NASA's Forgotten Machines to introduce school-age students to the spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments left across the Solar System. The platform features an interactive machine explorer covering the Moon, Mars, and deep space, with mission histories, scientific discoveries, images, timelines, and operational statuses.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming complex space exploration information into an engaging and easy-to-understand digital experience. Students can explore individual machines, learn why they were sent into space, discover what scientific knowledge they contributed, and understand whether they are still operating or inactive. An interactive quiz further encourages learning.

This project is important because these machines represent decades of human innovation and scientific discovery. By preserving and sharing their stories, we inspire the next generation to develop curiosity about space, science, engineering, and exploration.
details: NASA Hardware Explorer is an interactive website that tells the story of the equipment NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. A year slider (1960 to today) animates the planets and shows each spacecraft’s position, and clicking one reveals its status, its distance from Earth and how long a radio message takes to reach it, calculated from distance and the speed of light. It also includes a searchable mission library, a Voyager power simulator, a chart of how much longer the rovers lasted than planned, and a quiz, all supported by a written report. It helps school-age space enthusiasts explore ideas like light-travel time, nuclear power in space and mission lifetimes in a way a list of facts cannot, and it aims to spark curiosity about space engineering. I built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, drawing the map on the HTML canvas with no external libraries, using a laptop and a web browser, with help from Claude, an AI assistant, for drafting the code and report. Its creative idea is to turn hardware into a timeline you can scrub, so students can feel distance instead of reading numbers. I considered accuracy by using simplified orbits and approximate data that I label clearly, a plain-language style for the audience, and a lightweight single-file design that works on phones. The site also states that it is an independent educational project and not an official NASA website.
